longQuestions: An attribute is a qualitative characteristic that cannot be measured numerically but only noted as present or absent (blindness, literacy, honesty, gender).

Classification: by dichotomy (simple classification) — into two classes, possessing (A) and not possessing (α) the attribute; and manifold classification — into more than two classes (e.g. eye colour: blue, grey, brown); two-way classification uses two attributes at a time (contingency table).
i. Class symbol — a letter (A, B, α, β, AB, …) denoting a class; class frequency — the number of observations in that class, written in brackets, e.g. (A), (AB).
ii. Positive classes contain attributes A, B (presence); negative classes α, β (absence).
iii. Order of classes — the number of attributes specified: N is of order 0; (A), (α) of order 1; (AB), (Aβ) of order 2; and so on.
iv. Ultimate class frequencies — frequencies of the highest order, e.g. (AB), (Aβ), (αB), (αβ) for two attributes; all other frequencies can be found from them.
i. Two-way classification — classification of data by two attributes at the same time, giving a 2 × 2 (or r × c) table.
ii. Association of attributes — the tendency of two attributes to occur together more (or less) often than expected by chance.
iii. Positive association: (AB) > (A)(B)/N; negative association: (AB) < (A)(B)/N.
iv. Criterion of independence: A and B are independent if (AB) = (A)(B)/N, i.e. (AB)(αβ) = (Aβ)(αB).
v. Yule's coefficient of association Q = [(AB)(αβ) − (Aβ)(αB)]/[(AB)(αβ) + (Aβ)(αB)], ranging from −1 to +1.
Association measures the relationship between attributes (qualitative characteristics), using class frequencies and coefficients like Yule's Q or contingency coefficient.
Correlation measures the relationship between variables (quantitative, measurable) using actual values, with Karl Pearson's r ranging from −1 to +1.
i. Independent if (AB) = (A)(B)/N (equivalently Q = 0).
ii. Positively associated if (AB) > (A)(B)/N (Q > 0).
iii. Negatively associated if (AB) < (A)(B)/N (Q < 0).
i. Manifold classification — classification of data according to an attribute into more than two classes (e.g. A₁, A₂, …, A_r).
ii. (r × c) contingency table — a two-way table with r rows (classes of one attribute) and c columns (classes of the other), whose cells show observed frequencies.

iii. Chi-square distribution — the distribution of χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E, a continuous, positively skewed distribution from 0 to ∞ with parameter ν (degrees of freedom), used to test independence of attributes and goodness of fit.

Coefficient of mean square contingency: φ² = χ²/N; the coefficient of contingency C = √[χ²/(χ² + N)] measures the degree of association in an r × c table; it is 0 for independence and approaches (but never reaches) 1 for strong association; its maximum depends on the table size.
